title: Data structures and algorithm analysis introduction
learningObjectives: Explain what a data structure is and how it organizes values to support a defined set of operations.
Distinguish an abstract data type's behaviour from a particular in-memory representation.
Compare arrays, structures and pointer-linked nodes at a conceptual level, including contiguity and ownership.
Identify the operations a problem needs before selecting a representation.
Explain why time and auxiliary-space costs grow with input size, without confusing asymptotic growth with measured runtime.
Select a simple representation for a stated C problem and justify its trade-offs and constraints.

understand.concept: A data structure is a way of organizing data together with the operations used to access or modify it. An abstract data type (ADT) describes the behaviour and contract—such as push and pop—without requiring one particular memory layout. An implementation chooses concrete C objects, arrays, structures and pointers to provide that behaviour.
understand.whyItMatters: The same values can be stored in different ways, and each representation makes some operations simpler or more expensive. Choosing based on required operations, data size and lifetime is more reliable than choosing a structure because it is familiar.
understand.analogy: A set of customer records could be kept in numbered drawers, a linked chain of folders or an indexed catalogue. Each arrangement supports different ways of finding, inserting and removing records.
understand.analogyLimit: Physical filing analogies do not capture pointer validity, object lifetime, allocation failure, cache behaviour or the formal costs of C operations.

explain.narrative:
Start with the operations the program must support: access by position, search by key, insert, delete, traverse, or process in arrival order. An array stores elements contiguously and supports constant-time indexing when the index is valid, but inserting in the middle usually requires shifting elements. A linked structure connects separately stored nodes through pointers; insertion at a known link can be inexpensive, but traversal follows links and requires careful lifetime management.

A structure groups related fields into one object. An ADT is a contract, not a memory layout: a stack can be implemented with an array or a linked list while keeping the same last-in, first-out operations. Keep this distinction clear when discussing interfaces and implementations.

Algorithm analysis asks how an operation's work and extra memory grow as the input size grows. Count the dominant operations and state whether the estimate is best, average or worst case. Big-O describes an asymptotic upper bound, not seconds or a hardware benchmark. Later lessons examine specific growth classes and structures in detail.

examples.title: An array gives indexed access
examples.explanation: The array elements are contiguous and the program accesses one element by index after checking the bound. The count is derived from the array object rather than hard-coded. Once the array is passed to a function as a parameter, it is a pointer parameter and sizeof no longer gives the original array length.

examples.title: Separate an ADT contract from its representation
examples.code:
/* Stack ADT contract (representation-independent):
   push(x): add x to the top, or report full/failure
   pop(out): remove the top item, or report empty/failure
   peek(out): read the top item without removing it
   is_empty(): report whether there are no items

   Possible representations: fixed array + count,
   dynamically allocated array, or linked nodes. */
examples.explanation: The operations define observable behaviour. The implementation can change while callers continue to use the same contract, provided capacity, failure and ownership rules remain consistent.

practise.guidedTask: For a contact list, identify the operations users need: lookup by name, append, delete, iterate and access by position. Compare an array and linked list for those operations, stating what each representation makes easy or difficult.
practise.independentTask: Choose a data representation for a small queue of sensor readings with a known maximum capacity. State its operations, memory requirements, empty/full behaviour and why your choice fits the constraints.
hints: List required operations before choosing an implementation.
An ADT describes behaviour; an array or linked list is a possible representation.
Arrays are contiguous; linked nodes are separate objects connected by pointers.
Do not assume linked lists are automatically faster than arrays.
Include memory ownership and allocation failure in the design.
Big-O describes growth, not exact execution time.

questions.prompt: What does an abstract data type primarily specify?
options: The operations and their behaviour contract
The exact address of every object
The compiler's memory allocator
The syntax of a C loop
questions.answer: The operations and their behaviour contract
questions.explanation: An ADT describes what operations mean, not the only way to represent them.

questions.prompt: Which property is characteristic of a C array?
options: Its elements are stored contiguously
Every element has an independent allocation
It automatically grows when full
It stores elements of unrelated types
questions.explanation: C arrays are contiguous sequences of elements of one element type.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical trade-off of a linked list compared with an array?
options: Traversal follows links and indexed access is not constant-time
It always uses less memory
It guarantees faster search
It cannot be dynamically allocated
questions.answer: Traversal follows links and indexed access is not constant-time
questions.explanation: Linked lists require pointer traversal and per-node link storage.

questions.prompt: Why should required operations guide data-structure selection?
options: Different representations have different access, update and memory costs
All structures have identical behaviour and cost
The shortest type name is always best
The choice affects only printed formatting
questions.answer: Different representations have different access, update and memory costs
questions.explanation: A structure is useful when its operation profile matches the problem.

options: How resource use grows as input size increases
An exact runtime in milliseconds on every machine
The number of lines in the source file
The compiler version used
questions.answer: How resource use grows as input size increases
questions.explanation: Asymptotic analysis describes growth and abstracts away many machine-specific constants.
